text: Not every number you're capable of computing actually deserves a spot on a dashboard. Here's a genuinely reliable way to tell the difference before you build a single tile.

One test, applied metric by metric, every single time: if this number moved significantly, would anyone actually do anything differently because of it? If the honest answer is no, it's merely interesting, not actionable — and it belongs in a detailed report someone could drill into if they're curious, not among the handful of numbers somebody checks every single day.

A dashboard crowded with fifteen tiles doesn't actually communicate fifteen things — it communicates that nothing on it was worth prioritizing in the first place. Microsoft's own guidance is genuinely blunt here: keep it to one screen, avoid scrollbars entirely, and remove anything that isn't essential. Fewer, well-chosen KPIs consistently beat a longer list that just gets skimmed past without registering.

And a genuine KPI needs a real target to compare against, not just a raw value sitting there in isolation. Two point three million in sales this quarter means nothing on its own until you know whether that's above or below where it needed to be. That's exactly why the KPI visual exists as something distinct from a plain card — it's built specifically to show progress toward a defined goal.

Run every candidate through four quick questions: is it tied to a real goal, would it change a decision, does it have a target, and is it one of the handful needed at a glance. Next: dashboard layout and visual hierarchy — where the KPIs you just chose actually go on the page.
